teaser: An angel arrives with wonderful news. The woman he tells pulls her cloak shut and leans away.
review_notes:
Dimensions about 305 cm wide by 265 cm high: check.
Signed and dated 1333 by Simone Martini and Lippo Memmi (inscription preserved from the original frame); the attribution of the side saints to Lippo is a common guess, not a certainty.
Olive branch instead of lily because the lily was the emblem of Florence: traditional explanation, not documented.
The female saint is called Margaret in the catalog title; several scholars identify her as St. Maxima (Massima). The lesson mentions both.
The banner held by St. Ansanus is described as black and white (Siena's colors) from the image: check.
Frame is a 19th-century reconstruction; the central roundel is thought to have held God the Father.
Gabriel's robe: gold leaf under paint, scratched through (sgraffito): check.
Moved to Florence in 1799 by order of the Grand Duke of Tuscany, exchanged for two canvases by Luca Giordano: check.
Simone in Avignon from about 1336, friendship with Petrarch, lost portrait of Laura, death in 1344.
Luke's Gospel says Mary “was troubled” at the angel's words (Luke 1:29).

lesson.text: An angel has just landed, cloak still in the air, and kneels to deliver the most joyful message in the Christian story. The woman he speaks to twists away from him, pulls her cloak tight at the neck and frowns. The picture is about good news. Its heroine looks as if she wishes he would leave.

The scene is the Annunciation: the angel Gabriel tells Mary she will bear the son of God. The Gospel of Luke adds a small human detail, that she was “troubled” by his greeting. Most painters jumped ahead to her calm acceptance. Simone Martini stops the clock one second earlier.
The whole drama fits in the narrow space between two bodies.

lines.label: Leaning in
lines.text: Gabriel's body rises in one eager slant from knee to face. Everything about him presses toward her.

lines.label: The sentence
lines.text: His words leave his mouth as raised golden letters and cross the gap in a straight line, aimed at her ear.

lines.label: Pulling back
lines.text: Mary answers with a long S-curve. Head tilted one way, shoulder turned the other, knees swinging back toward us. Her body says no while her face is still deciding.

lines.label: The divider
lines.text: A vase of lilies stands exactly between them, on the picture's central axis. He does not cross it.

lesson.text: Those letters are real. Built up in relief and gilded, they spell AVE GRATIA PLENA DOMINUS TECUM, Latin for “Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with you.” Speech travels across the gold like a caption in a comic strip, six centuries before comic strips.

Two men signed this painting. An inscription on the frame names Simone Martini and his brother-in-law Lippo Memmi, with the year 1333. Experts have argued ever since about who painted what. The usual guess gives the two saints at the sides to Lippo.

It was made for the cathedral of Siena, for the altar of St. Ansanus, one of the city's patron saints. The whole thing is about 3 meters wide (10 feet). There is no room in it, no wall, no window: only gold. And yet the few objects Simone allows in are painted with a sharp, almost nosy realism.

lesson.title: Solid things, nowhere
lesson.text: Three objects that insist on being real.

spots.title: Lilies in a vase
spots.text: White lilies, the flower of Mary's purity, with stiff stems and a few drooping heads. The golden vase has two handles and sits firmly on the floor.

spots.title: The book
spots.text: She was reading when he arrived. Her thumb is tucked between the pages of the red book to keep her place, as if she expects to return to it.

spots.title: The cloak
spots.text: Gabriel's mantle still whips out behind him, showing a checked lining like a tartan. It has not had time to fall. He touched down an instant ago.

lesson.text: So the picture holds a second contradiction. The setting is flat, timeless gold, the old way of showing heaven. The marble floor, the vase and the bookmark thumb belong to a real afternoon. Simone refuses to choose between the two, and the tension is part of the charm.

What ties it together is line. Painters in Siena loved a long, elegant contour, the taste of the Gothic age that also shaped French ivories and illuminated books. See how thin Mary's fingers are, how her dark cloak is cut out against the gold like a single ink stroke.
One more oddity. In most Annunciations, Gabriel carries a lily. Here the lilies have been moved to the vase, and the angel brings a different plant. He is also wearing it.
Find the branch Gabriel holds out to Mary.

spots.title: Olive
spots.text: It is an olive branch, a sign of peace, and a wreath of the same leaves circles his hair. An old explanation: the lily was the emblem of Florence, Siena's great rival, so Sienese angels avoided carrying it.

lesson.text: Simone Martini paints a feeling in the middle of changing. Mary has not yet said yes, and that hesitation makes the scene believable.

The shimmer is craft. For Gabriel's robe, the painters laid gold leaf, covered it with paint, then scratched the paint away in tiny patterns so the gold shows through. The halos were stamped with small metal punches. In a cathedral lit by candles, every dent would catch a moving flame.

The spiky gilded frame is not medieval. The original was lost, and what you see was built in the 1800s. The empty circle at the very top is thought to have once held a figure of God the Father, sending the dove below.

The side panels belong to the altar more than to the story. On the left stands Ansanus, a young martyr, with a banner. The woman on the right is traditionally called Margaret, though some scholars think she is Maxima, the saint who raised him. Wander around the whole structure.

spots.title: Mary's face
spots.text: Eyes narrowed, mouth turned down, chin tucked into her shoulder. It is one of the least flattering and most human expressions given to Mary in medieval art.

spots.title: Gabriel's face
spots.text: Lips parted in mid-word, olive leaves in his hair. His profile is as sharp as a face on a coin.

spots.title: The dove
spots.text: The Holy Spirit descends as a dove inside a ring of winged cherubs, whose pointed wings fan out like a star.

spots.title: St. Ansanus
spots.text: Siena's young patron holds a banner and a martyr's palm. He stands on his own patch of ground, in his own arch, apart from the event.

spots.title: The woman saint
spots.text: Wrapped in gray-violet, she carries a cross and a palm. Her face is rounder and more heavily shaded than Mary's, one reason the side saints are often given to Lippo Memmi.

spots.title: A prophet
spots.text: Four roundels above hold Old Testament prophets with scrolls. They are there as witnesses: their writings were read as predictions of this moment.

spots.title: The empty circle
spots.text: A blank disk of gold where an image once sat. The frame around it is a nineteenth-century replacement.

lesson.text: A few years later Simone left Siena for Avignon, in southern France, where the popes were then living. There he became a friend of the poet Petrarch, who praised him in two sonnets for a portrait of his beloved Laura. That portrait is lost. Simone died in Avignon in 1344.

The altarpiece itself ended up with the enemy. In 1799 the ruler of Tuscany had it carried off to Florence, and Siena's cathedral received two later canvases in exchange. The angel who would not carry a Florentine lily has hung in Florence ever since.

quiz.question: How does Mary react to the angel in this painting?
options: She kneels and opens her arms
She shrinks back and pulls her cloak closed
She keeps reading and ignores him
quiz.explanation: Simone shows the moment when, as Luke's Gospel says, she is troubled by the greeting.

quiz.question: How are Gabriel's words shown?
options: As raised golden letters crossing the space
quiz.explanation: The Latin greeting runs in gilded relief from his mouth toward Mary.

quiz.question: What plant does Gabriel hold?
quiz.explanation: He carries olive, a sign of peace, and wears an olive wreath too.

quiz.question: What detail shows that Mary was interrupted?
options: A candle has just gone out
Her thumb marks her place in a book
A spindle has dropped to the floor
quiz.explanation: Her thumb is tucked between the pages of the red book.

quiz.question: Who signed the altarpiece with Simone Martini?
quiz.explanation: The frame inscription names both painters and the year 1333.

quiz.question: Where did Simone spend his last years?
quiz.explanation: He moved to Avignon, where the popes lived, and died there in 1344.

facts.text: The gilded frame with its pinnacles dates from Simone Martini's time.
facts.explanation: The original frame was lost, and the present one was made in the 1800s.

facts.text: The altarpiece was painted for the cathedral of Siena.
facts.explanation: It stood on the altar of St. Ansanus, one of the city's patron saints.

facts.text: The scene is set in a detailed bedroom with a window and a bed.
facts.explanation: The background is plain gold, with only a floor, a vase and a throne.
